questions.question: A family physician incorporates a validated single-question screening tool into intake visits: "Do you ever have difficulty making ends meet at the end of the month?" For identifying patients living below the poverty line, this question has a sensitivity of 98% and a specificity of 40%. Which statement best describes how this screening question performs?

options.text: It correctly identifies almost all patients who are truly living in poverty, but many patients who are not living in poverty will also screen positive
It correctly identifies almost all patients who are not living in poverty, while missing many who are living in poverty
It performs equally well at detecting patients with and without poverty
A positive answer to this question, by itself, confirms that the patient is living in poverty
Because specificity is high, very few patients who are not living in poverty will answer yes to this question

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes reports that this poverty-screening question has a sensitivity of 98% and a specificity of 40% for identifying patients below the poverty line. Very high sensitivity means very few false negatives, so almost all true cases are detected, but a specificity of only 40% means a large share of people without the condition will still test positive (many false positives), which matches option a.

optionExplanations.b: This describes a test with high specificity and low sensitivity, the opposite of the 98% sensitivity/40% specificity reported for this question.
optionExplanations.c: Sensitivity (98%) and specificity (40%) are markedly different, so the question does not perform equally in both directions.
optionExplanations.d: A screening test result is not diagnostic; with only 40% specificity, many patients without poverty will still screen positive, so a positive answer alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.
optionExplanations.e: Specificity here is only 40%, not high, so a substantial proportion of patients who are not living in poverty will still answer yes.

questions.question: During an investigation of a suspected outbreak of a novel respiratory pathogen, the public health unit does not wait for cases to be voluntarily reported by clinicians. Instead, staff conduct scheduled visits to hospitals and clinics to actively review medical records and test patients, in order to identify every possible case in the affected area. Which type of surveillance does this best describe?
questions.explanation: The source defines active surveillance as regular visits to health facilities to review records or actively test for a disease under surveillance, used when every possible case must be investigated, such as during outbreak investigations. Although resource-intensive, this fits the scenario because the unit is deliberately seeking out every case rather than relying on voluntary reporting.

optionExplanations.a: Passive surveillance relies on institutions and clinicians to report cases on their own, rather than public health staff actively seeking out cases.
optionExplanations.c: Sentinel surveillance uses a limited network of pre-selected reporting sites to signal trends, not comprehensive active case-finding across an affected area.
optionExplanations.d: A case-control study samples people based on outcome status to compare exposures; it is a research design, not an ongoing surveillance method.
optionExplanations.e: A cross-sectional survey collects exposure and outcome data on individuals at a single point in time; it is a research design, not an ongoing surveillance system.

questions.question: A new screening program detects a slow-growing cancer several years earlier than it would have been diagnosed after the onset of symptoms. Because survival time is now measured starting from the earlier screening date rather than from the later date of clinical presentation, patients whose disease was found by screening appear to survive longer after diagnosis, even though screening did not actually delay the time of death. Which bias explains this apparent improvement in survival time?
questions.explanation: The source defines lead-time bias as overestimation of survival time from diagnosis when the estimate is made from the time of screening instead of the later time at which the disease would have been diagnosed without screening. In this scenario, the earlier diagnosis date artificially lengthens the measured survival interval without changing the actual time of death.

optionExplanations.b: Length-time bias results from screening being more likely to detect slow-growing, indolent cases than aggressive ones; it does not describe shifting the starting point at which survival is measured.
optionExplanations.c: Selection bias arises from how participants are recruited or retained in a study, not from the timing of diagnosis relative to symptom onset.
optionExplanations.d: Recall bias arises when individuals with disease more readily recall a past exposure than those without disease; it does not describe a shift in when survival time starts being measured.
optionExplanations.e: Confounding involves a third variable related to both exposure and outcome; it is unrelated to how survival time is measured.

questions.question: Investigators conduct a case-control study examining the association between a chronic occupational exposure and a respiratory disease. Cases are recruited from patients admitted to a tertiary hospital respirology ward. Controls are recruited from patients admitted to the same hospital for unrelated surgical procedures. Both cases and controls may have been admitted, in part, because of factors related to their overall health complexity rather than being representative of the general population. Which type of bias is most likely to affect this study?
questions.explanation: The source states that Berkson's bias occurs in a case-control study that uses hospitalized controls, because hospitalized patients may not be a representative sample due to the complexity of factors that led to their admission. Since both the cases and controls here are drawn from hospitalized patients whose admission itself may relate to unmeasured health factors, the study is at risk of Berkson's bias.

optionExplanations.b: Recall bias occurs when cases and controls differ in how accurately they remember past exposures, not when controls are drawn from a non-representative hospitalized population.
optionExplanations.c: Non-response bias occurs when people who agree to participate differ systematically from those who decline, which is not the issue described here.
optionExplanations.d: Loss to follow-up bias occurs when participants drop out differentially between groups during a study, which does not apply to this recruitment of cases and controls.
optionExplanations.e: Interviewer bias occurs when unblinded interviewers behave differently based on knowledge of outcome status, which is not what is described in this recruitment scenario.

questions.question: In a randomized trial comparing a new drug to placebo for a chronic disease, 30% of patients in the placebo (control) group died during follow-up, compared with 20% of patients who received the new drug. Using the definitions of absolute risk reduction and number needed to treat presented in this source, what is the number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one additional death?
questions.explanation: The source defines absolute risk reduction (ARR) as CER minus EER and NNT as 1/ARR. Here, ARR = 30% − 20% = 10%, so NNT = 1/0.10 = 10, meaning 10 patients would need to be treated with the new drug to prevent one additional death compared with placebo.

optionExplanations.a: This would result if ARR were 20%, double the actual 10% difference between the groups.
optionExplanations.c: This value does not correspond to 1/ARR using the event rates given in this scenario.
optionExplanations.d: This equals the experimental group's event rate (20%), not 1/ARR.
optionExplanations.e: This equals the control group's event rate (30%), not 1/ARR.

questions.question: Researchers want to study whether a specific occupational chemical exposure increases the risk of a rare form of bladder cancer. They begin by identifying patients recently diagnosed with this cancer at several hospitals, along with a comparable group of patients without the cancer, and then interview both groups about their past occupational exposures. Which observational study design is being used?
questions.explanation: The source describes case-control studies as sampling a group of people who already have a particular outcome (cases) and comparing them to a similar sample without that outcome (controls), then assessing past exposures. It also notes this design is often used when the disease of interest is rare, which matches both the method and the rare-cancer context in this vignette.

optionExplanations.a: An ecological study analyzes populations or groups rather than individuals, and does not sample based on individual disease status as in this scenario.
optionExplanations.b: A cross-sectional study collects exposure and outcome data on individuals at a single point in time without first selecting groups based on outcome status.
optionExplanations.d: A cohort study begins by classifying individuals as exposed or unexposed and follows them forward to observe outcomes, rather than starting with people who already have or do not have the disease.
optionExplanations.e: A randomized controlled trial involves randomly allocating participants to an intervention or control group; there is no such allocation described here.

questions.question: In a clinical trial testing a new antihypertensive medication, participants are unaware of whether they are receiving the study drug or placebo, and the researchers assessing participants' blood pressure outcomes are also unaware of each participant's group assignment. Neither the participants nor the outcome assessors know the treatment allocation. What is this method of assessment called?
questions.explanation: The source defines double-blind as a method in which both the participant and the observer are unaware of group assignment, which matches this scenario where neither the patient nor the person assessing blood pressure knows whether the drug or placebo was given.

optionExplanations.a: Single-blind means only the participant is unaware of group assignment, whereas here both the participant and the observer are unaware.
optionExplanations.c: Triple-blind requires that the participant, observer, and analyst all be unaware of group assignment; the scenario does not describe the data analyst's blinding status.
optionExplanations.d: An open-label trial is one in which participants and researchers know the treatment assignment, the opposite of what is described here.
optionExplanations.e: Intention-to-treat analysis is a method of analyzing outcomes according to original group assignment regardless of adherence; it is unrelated to blinding of participants and assessors.

source.reference: PH18 — Experimental Study Designs (Randomized Controlled Trial)

questions.question: A physician diagnoses a patient with measles and is required by provincial law to report this to the local public health unit, even though the case is a single patient with no evidence yet of further spread in the community. Which of the following is a reason given for making disease reporting mandatory in this context?

options.text: To identify and control an outbreak
To provide the patient with financial compensation for lost income
To determine legal liability for the source of the patient's infection
To assign the patient's case to a specific insurance category
To fulfill workplace safety inspection requirements

questions.explanation: The source lists reasons mandatory reporting is required, including to identify and control an outbreak, to prevent spread when a disease poses a significant threat, and for surveillance to monitor disease trends over time. Reporting an individual case of measles supports early identification and control of a potential outbreak, even before spread is confirmed.

optionExplanations.b: Financial compensation for lost income is unrelated to the stated purposes of mandatory disease reporting in this source.
optionExplanations.c: Determining legal liability is not among the reasons given for mandatory reporting in this source.
optionExplanations.d: Assigning an insurance category is not a purpose of mandatory disease reporting described in this source.
optionExplanations.e: Workplace safety inspections are a separate occupational health function, not a stated reason for mandatory infectious disease reporting.

questions.question: A local public health unit is investigating a multi-province cluster of salmonellosis traced to a brand of frozen breaded chicken product still on grocery shelves. The medical officer of health wants the implicated product recalled from sale across Canada. Which organization holds the federal responsibility for food safety, labelling, and recalls?

options.text: The provincial public health agency (e.g. Public Health Ontario)

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes divides public health legislation and responsibility between federal and provincial bodies. Federally, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency regulates federal food safety, labelling, and recalls, and deals with animal-related infections. A national recall of a contaminated food product is therefore a CFIA function, even though the outbreak investigation and follow-up of reported disease are carried out locally.

optionExplanations.a: Health Canada approves new drugs and medical devices, provides non-insured health benefits to status First Nations peoples and Inuit, and publishes Canada's Food Guide, but does not run food recalls.
optionExplanations.b: The Public Health Agency of Canada is the main federal agency responsible for public health and was created post-SARS; it responds to outbreaks and emergencies but does not regulate food labelling and recalls.
optionExplanations.d: The Canadian Institutes of Health Research was formed in 2000 to support research to improve health and the health care system; it has no regulatory role.
optionExplanations.e: Provincial agencies operate under each province's Public Health Act and support local units; recall of a federally regulated food product is not within provincial jurisdiction.

source.reference: PH3 — Legislation and Public Health in Canada

questions.question: A medical officer of health is concerned about rising rates of childhood obesity in her catchment area. She presents local data to municipal council and successfully advocates for a by-law that removes sugar-sweetened beverages from vending machines in all city-owned recreation centres and arenas. Under the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion (1986), which action does this best represent?
questions.explanation: The Ottawa Charter states that governments and health care providers should be involved in a health promotion process that includes building healthy public policy, creating supportive environments, strengthening community action, developing personal skills, and re-orienting health services. Enacting a municipal by-law is legislative action at the level of government, which is the defining feature of building healthy public policy. Most health promotion is done at the population level by public health professionals and agencies through engaging stakeholders, formulating policy, and influencing upstream factors.

optionExplanations.b: Creating supportive environments refers to shaping the physical and social settings people live in rather than to the legislative act of passing a by-law; here the mechanism is policy formulation.
optionExplanations.c: Strengthening community action would involve mobilizing community groups to set and act on their own priorities, which is not what the medical officer of health did.
optionExplanations.d: Developing personal skills refers to health education that increases individual knowledge and capability, not to municipal legislation.
optionExplanations.e: Re-orienting health services refers to shifting the health care system itself toward prevention and promotion, not to a municipal by-law on vending machines.

source.reference: PH4 — Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion

questions.question: A provincial ministry is ranking chronic conditions in order to set funding priorities. It wants a single summary measure that counts both the years lost due to premature mortality and the years lost due to disability, whether the disability is physical or mental, so that a disabling but rarely fatal condition is not ranked as harmless. Which measure best meets this requirement?
questions.explanation: A disability adjusted life year is the number of years lost due to premature mortality plus the number of years lost due to disability, where 0 is a year of perfect health and 1 is death, and those disabilities can be physical or mental. Because it accounts for both premature death and time spent with disability, the DALY is the measure used to assess the burden of diseases in a population. The other options capture only mortality or serve an economic rather than a burden-of-disease purpose.

optionExplanations.b: A QALY weights years of life by quality, from 0 (death) to 1 (perfect health), and is usually used as an economic measure to assess the value for money of medical interventions.
optionExplanations.c: PYLL is calculated from the difference between the actual age at death and a standard or expected age at death, giving increased weighting to mortality at a younger age; it ignores disability.
optionExplanations.d: The SMR is observed deaths divided by expected deaths, an indirectly standardized mortality comparison rather than a measure of disease burden including disability.
optionExplanations.e: The IMR counts reported deaths among children under 1 yr of age per 1000 live births and is a specific mortality indicator.

questions.question: A provincial registry has followed a chronic neurological disease for 15 yr. The number of new cases identified each year in the population has remained essentially unchanged over that period, yet point prevalence has nearly doubled. During the same interval a treatment was introduced that does not cure the disease but substantially prolongs survival. Which statement best explains the registry's findings?

options.text: The incidence rate must in fact have increased, since the number of new cases in a population over a specific period of time drives prevalence
Prevalence is a function of the incidence rate and of disease duration from onset to termination, so longer survival alone can raise prevalence
The registry has switched from reporting point prevalence to period prevalence, which includes new cases and excludes cases that terminate
Prevalence is underestimating the true disease burden because cases with short disease duration are being missed
The apparent rise is an artefact of the crude rate and would disappear once the rate was age-standardized to a standard population

questions.explanation: The incidence rate is the number of new cases in a population over a specific period of time, whereas prevalence is the total number of cases and is a function of the incidence rate and disease duration from onset to termination. A treatment that prolongs survival without curing lengthens duration, so cases accumulate and prevalence rises even with a flat incidence rate. This is also why prevalence favours the inclusion of chronic over acute cases and is used to measure disease burden for planning facilities and services.

optionExplanations.a: The registry counts new cases directly; a stable count of new cases means the incidence rate has not changed, and prevalence can rise without it.
optionExplanations.c: Point prevalence is assessed at one point in time and period prevalence over a period of time; a change in which is reported would not by itself double the estimate, and the stem states point prevalence was measured throughout.
optionExplanations.d: This statement is true of prevalence in general but describes underestimation of burden from short-duration cases, which would lower rather than raise the measured prevalence.
optionExplanations.e: Age standardization adjusts a crude rate using a standard population to allow comparison between dissimilar populations; nothing in the stem indicates a shift in age distribution.

questions.question: A 58-year-old lifelong non-smoker is diagnosed with lung cancer. She lives alone in a rural house and sleeps in a finished basement bedroom; no one has ever smoked in the home and she has had no occupational dust or asbestos exposure. Her physician takes an environmental health history and notes that the local soil contains uranium. Which indoor air exposure most likely contributed to her cancer?
questions.explanation: Radon is an ionizing radiation hazard that is naturally produced by soil containing uranium or radium and can contaminate indoor air; it is associated with approximately 20% of lung cancers. A basement sleeping area in a region with uranium-bearing soil is exactly the reservoir and route this describes, and the other indoor and outdoor air hazards listed on this page act mainly as airway irritants or systemic toxins.

optionExplanations.b: Ground-level ozone is the main component of smog, an outdoor chemical hazard that worsens asthma and irritates the upper airway.
optionExplanations.c: Carbon monoxide is a common byproduct of combustion that aggravates cardiac disease at low levels, causes headache, nausea, and dizziness at moderate levels, and is fatal at high levels.
optionExplanations.d: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are fossil-fuel related, contribute to acid rain, and exacerbate breathing difficulties rather than causing lung cancer.
optionExplanations.e: Second-hand tobacco smoke does increase the risk of lung cancer, but the history states that no one has ever smoked in the home.

questions.question: A trial of a community salt-reduction program reports a mean reduction in systolic blood pressure of 12 mmHg compared with usual care (95% CI 8 to 16 mmHg). A resident asks how this interval should be read. Which statement is the best interpretation of the reported confidence interval?

options.text: 95% of participants in the program had a blood pressure reduction between 8 and 16 mmHg
It is a range bound by upper and lower confidence limits containing the true population parameter; if the study were repeated 100 times, the 95% CI would contain that parameter 95 out of 100 times
There is a 95% probability that the null hypothesis of no difference is false
For the same critical value, a wider interval would indicate less variance in the data than a tighter interval
Because the interval excludes zero, the observed reduction must also be clinically significant

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines a confidence interval as a range of values, bound by the upper and lower confidence limits, that contains the true population parameter, and explains a 95% CI as meaning that if the study were repeated 100 times the interval would contain the population parameter 95 out of 100 times. The interval describes the precision of the estimate of the population parameter, not the spread of individual patients' responses.

optionExplanations.a: A confidence interval bounds the population parameter such as the mean; it is not a range within which a given percentage of individual observations fall.
optionExplanations.c: The probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis is denoted by the p-value; a confidence interval is not a probability statement about the null hypothesis.
optionExplanations.d: This is reversed: a wider confidence interval implies more variance than a tighter confidence interval given the same critical value.
optionExplanations.e: Statistical significance does not establish clinical significance; the source notes a 1 mmHg blood pressure reduction may be statistically significant yet not clinically useful once cost, availability, adherence, and side effects are considered.

questions.question: An outbreak of a diarrhoeal illness occurs in a town of 20 000 people. Over six weeks the public health unit identifies 400 people with the illness, of whom 12 die as a result of it. Using these figures, what is the case-fatality rate?
questions.explanation: The case-fatality rate is the proportion of individuals with the disease who died as a result of the illness during a specified time period, calculated as (number of cases that died / total number of cases) x 100%. Here that is (12/400) x 100% = 3%. The CFR must be clearly differentiated from the mortality rate, which is the proportion of the whole population that died during the period.

optionExplanations.a: 0.06% is 12/20 000, the crude mortality rate for the town, not the case-fatality rate.
optionExplanations.b: 2% is 400/20 000, the attack rate: the proportion of an initially disease-free population that develops the disease over a specified time period.
optionExplanations.d: 25% does not correspond to any of the numbers given and would require 100 deaths among the 400 cases.
optionExplanations.e: 30% would be the result of dividing by the number of deaths rather than by the total number of cases.

questions.question: A public health unit receives a report of a vomiting illness among members of a baseball team after a team dinner at a restaurant. The investigation team has been assembled, the observed number of cases has been compared with the number expected during a non-outbreak time frame to establish that an outbreak exists, and medical records and laboratory reports have been obtained to verify the diagnosis. According to the ten-step approach to controlling an outbreak, what should the team do next?

options.text: Define a case in terms of person, place, and time
Create a line list containing clinical, demographic, and exposure information for each case
Perform descriptive epidemiology and construct an epidemic curve
Conduct a case-control study to evaluate hypotheses about the exposure
Involve the media to address public concerns and call for public action

questions.explanation: In the ten-step approach, once the investigation team is identified, the existence of an outbreak is established, and the diagnosis is verified, the next step is to define a case. A case definition has three components — person, place, and time — and it must exist before cases can be found systematically, because it determines who counts as a case for the line list and all later analysis.

optionExplanations.b: Finding cases systemically and creating a line list is the following step, and it cannot be done consistently until a case definition exists.
optionExplanations.c: Descriptive epidemiology and epidemic curves come after cases have been found and listed, and are used to develop hypotheses.
optionExplanations.d: Evaluating hypotheses with a case-control study, useful when not everyone exposed can be found and included, comes later in the ten-step sequence.
optionExplanations.e: Communicating findings, including involving the media, is one of the final steps once the investigation has produced findings to communicate.

source.reference: PH25 — Steps to Control an Outbreak

questions.question: An occupational medicine physician is consulted about a metal fabrication shop where several workers have developed irritant contact dermatitis and headaches from a degreasing solvent. Safety data sheets confirm the solvent is the likely hazard, and a less hazardous water-based product could do the same job. Applying the hierarchy of controls for reduction of occupational exposures, which measure should be recommended as the most effective?

options.text: Remove the solvent from the process entirely by switching to the water-based product
Install local exhaust ventilation over the degreasing station to isolate workers from the hazard
Rotate workers through the degreasing station to limit each person's duration of contact
Issue chemical-resistant gloves and fit-tested respirators to all workers at the station
Provide annual training on reading safety data sheets and on symptoms of solvent exposure

questions.explanation: The hierarchy of controls ranks measures from most to least effective: elimination of the hazard, then substitution and engineering controls that isolate people from the hazard, then administrative controls that change the way people work, then personal protective equipment as the least effective option. Eliminating the solvent by replacing it with a less hazardous product removes the exposure at its source rather than relying on the worker, so it sits at the top of the hierarchy. This is also primary prevention, the recognition and control of exposure to hazards.

optionExplanations.b: Ventilation is an engineering control that isolates the worker from the hazard; effective, but ranked below removing the hazard altogether.
optionExplanations.c: Job rotation is an administrative control that changes the way people work and still leaves every worker exposed for part of the time.
optionExplanations.d: Gloves and respirators are personal protective equipment, the least effective level of the hierarchy because protection depends on correct and continuous use.
optionExplanations.e: Education about safety data sheets is an administrative control; it informs workers but does not reduce the exposure itself.

questions.question: A 52-year-old family physician runs a solo practice in a town that has flooded twice in the past decade. The municipality already has a provincial emergency response plan and a centralized facility to coordinate the entire response to a disaster. She now wants a document setting out guidelines on how her office's critical functions and services would be maintained if the next flood closed her building for weeks. Which of the following is the next best step for her practice?

options.text: Develop a Continuity of Operations Plan (COOP)
Develop a second Emergency Response Plan (ERP) for the practice
Adopt an Incident Management System (IMS) for the practice
Designate an Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) for the practice
Implement an early detection system and disaster preparedness program

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes separates the disaster-management instruments by purpose: a Continuity of Operations Plan provides guidelines on how critical functions and services will be maintained in the event of a disaster, and gives maintaining the operations of a physician's office during a disaster as its own example. What this physician is asking for is exactly that — continuity of her practice's critical functions and services — rather than coordination of the municipality's overall response, so a COOP is the document to develop.

optionExplanations.b: An Emergency Response Plan outlines the policies, procedures, roles, and responsibilities of various parties to coordinate action; the municipality already has one, and it does not address how her own critical services continue.
optionExplanations.c: An Incident Management System applies during the response phase, standardizing responses to an incident across personnel, facilities, equipment, financing, procedures, and public information communications — not sustaining routine services.
optionExplanations.d: An Emergency Operations Centre is a centralized facility or location to coordinate the entire response to a disaster; the stem states one already exists, and it is a site rather than a plan for her practice.
optionExplanations.e: Early detection systems and disaster preparedness programs mitigate disasters before they occur, but they do not specify how her critical functions and services would be maintained once one has occurred.

source.reference: PH30 — Disaster Preparedness, Emergency Response, and Recovery
